The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$ and let $\mathbb T^d=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^d$ carry normalized product Haar measure $dx$, with $dx(\mathbb T^d)=1$. Coordinates and time are dimensionless in the diffusive normalization $D=1$. For $r\in(0,1)$ set the mobility function $\chi(r):=r(1-r)$. Require both fields to be smooth up to the time endpoints and periodic in space, and require that for some $\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)$, $\varepsilon\le\rho(t,x)\le1-\varepsilon$ for every $(t,x)$. Call $(\rho,j)$ admissible when it also satisfies the continuity equation $\partial_t\rho+\nabla\cdot j=0$. Define its dimensionless action by

$$\mathcal I_{[a,b]}(\rho,j):=\frac14\int_a^b\int_{\mathbb T^d}\frac{|j(t,x)+\nabla\rho(t,x)|^2}{\rho(t,x)(1-\rho(t,x))}\,dx\,dt.$$

This is the macroscopic fluctuation functional in the stated normalized SSEP coefficient convention. It is a definition of a functional and does not assert a microscopic path-space large-deviation principle or a probability estimate.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$ and let $\rho_0:\mathbb T^d\to\mathbb R$ be measurable with $0\le\rho_0\le1$ almost everywhere, using normalized product Haar measure $dx$. For $k\in\mathbb Z^d$ define $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i k\cdot x)$ and $\widehat f(k)=\int_{\mathbb T^d}f(x)e_{-k}(x)\,dx$. For $t>0$ set

$$\rho_t(x):=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}e^{-4\pi^2|k|^2t}\widehat\rho_0(k)e_k(x),$$

and at $t=0$ set $\rho_t=\rho_0$ as an almost-everywhere class. For smooth periodic $G$, define

$$P_tG(x):=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}e^{-4\pi^2|k|^2t}\widehat G(k)e_k(x)\quad(t>0),\qquad P_0G:=G.$$

Then on every strip $[\epsilon,T]\times\mathbb T^d$ with $0<\epsilon<T<\infty$, the series for $\rho_t$ and all its space and time derivatives converge absolutely and uniformly; in particular $\rho_t$ is real and smooth for each $t>0$ and $\partial_t\rho_t=\Delta\rho_t$. For every finite $T$ and every smooth $G$, $P_tG$ is smooth on $[0,T]\times\mathbb T^d$, satisfies $\partial_tP_tG=\Delta P_tG$, has uniformly bounded derivatives of every fixed order there, and $P_tG\to G$ uniformly as $t\downarrow0$. derivations.claim: For the coordinate observables, the generator gives $L\eta_1=\alpha+\eta_2-2\eta_1$ and $L\eta_2=\beta+\eta_1-2\eta_2$. If $\pi$ is stationary and $m_i:=\mathbb E_\pi\eta_i$, then $\mathbb E_\pi L\eta_i=0$, so $2m_1-m_2=\alpha$ and $2m_2-m_1=\beta$. Solving gives $m_1=(2\alpha+\beta)/3$ and $m_2=(\alpha+2\beta)/3$.

Let $q:=\mathbb E_\pi(\eta_1\eta_2)$. The swap does not change $\eta_1\eta_2$, and the two reservoir flips give $L(\eta_1\eta_2)=\alpha\eta_2+\beta\eta_1-2\eta_1\eta_2$. Stationarity therefore yields $2q=\alpha m_2+\beta m_1$, hence $q=(\alpha^2+4\alpha\beta+\beta^2)/6$.

Substituting the moments from steps 1.1 and 2.1 gives $q-m_1m_2=\frac{\alpha^2+4\alpha\beta+\beta^2}{6}-\frac{(2\alpha+\beta)(\alpha+2\beta)}{9}=-\frac{(\alpha-\beta)^2}{18}$. If $\alpha\ne\beta$, this covariance is nonzero, whereas two independent Bernoulli occupations have zero covariance; thus $\pi$ is not a product law.

Define probabilities by $\pi_{11}=q$, $\pi_{10}=m_1-q$, $\pi_{01}=m_2-q$, and $\pi_{00}=1-m_1-m_2+q$. They sum to one; $\pi_{11}>0$ and $\pi_{00}=[(1-\alpha)^2+4(1-\alpha)(1-\beta)+(1-\beta)^2]/6>0$. For fixed $\beta$, $6\pi_{10}=g(\alpha)$ where $g(a)=a(4-4\beta-a)+\beta(2-\beta)$ is concave on $[0,1]$ and has positive endpoint values $g(0)=\beta(2-\beta)$ and $g(1)=(1-\beta)(3+\beta)$; hence $\pi_{10}>0$. By interchanging $\alpha$ and $\beta$ the same argument gives $\pi_{01}>0$.

The probabilities in step 3.2 have the moments in steps 1.1 and 2.1, so their expectation of $L$ vanishes on $1,\eta_1,\eta_2,\eta_1\eta_2$. These four functions form a basis of all real functions on $\Omega$, hence the probability vector is stationary. Conversely, every stationary law must satisfy the same three moment equations, which determine $m_1,m_2,q$ uniquely and then determine all four atom probabilities; therefore this stationary law is unique. If $\alpha=\beta=r$, the same probabilities reduce to $\pi_{00}=(1-r)^2$, $\pi_{10}=\pi_{01}=r(1-r)$, and $\pi_{11}=r^2$, the product Bernoulli law. Step 3.1 gives the claimed covariance.
